title: Yitro: on eagles' wings (Exodus 19:4)
hookLine: "I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself"

lines: HOW DID YOU GET THROUGH IT?
cards: Ask someone how they got through the worst year of their life, and sometimes the answer isn't I was strong. It's: my sister moved in. My friends set up a meal schedule.
My grandmother called every single night. Some people see only later that they were carried; at the time they were too busy surviving. Moses climbs the mountain.
Before any commandment, before any thunder, God gives him a message for the people. And it begins by asking them to look back at how they got here.

teach.h: WHAT I DID, HOW I BORE YOU, TO ME.
teach.b: Here it is, in the old Jewish translation: "Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself."
Three things in one breath: what happened to Egypt, how you were carried, and where you were carried to. Not to a place, but to Me. Rashi, drawing on the Mekhilta, asks: why an eagle?

teach.h: OTHER BIRDS CARRY IN THEIR CLAWS.
teach.b: Other birds, he says, carry their young in their claws, because they fear the bigger birds above them. The eagle flies higher than any of them, so the only danger comes from below, from a hunter's arrow.
So the eagle carries its young on its wings.
Let the arrow strike me, the eagle says, rather than my children. That's the picture the verse paints: a parent putting itself between the danger and the little one.
The Torah uses the image again near its end, in the song of Moses in Deuteronomy, where an eagle stirs up her nest, hovers over her young, spreads her wings and carries them.
One honest note: the Hebrew word, nesher, may mean a griffon vulture as much as an eagle; scholars debate it.
Either way, it's a huge bird with a long reach. And the people the verse speaks to were carried before they knew it, through plagues and the sea and the desert, to the foot of this mountain.

how: Jewish teachers read Exodus 19:4 alongside Rashi's comment on the eagle shielding its young, and the image returns in the song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32:11.

games.q: you're an eagle carrying your young. the only danger is an arrow from below. where do you carry them?
o: you leave them in the nest.
games.why: on your wings. Rashi, after the Mekhilta: let the arrow strike me rather than my children.

practice: Think of a hard stretch that's behind you now, and let the faces or names of those who carried you through it come, one by one: a person, a stranger, a teacher, a song, a community. Some of them you may never have thanked.
If you pray, you can give thanks for them now; if not, stay with the names, and how much of the weight was shared.

wordCard.voice: Yitro. Our portion, where God's first message at Sinai reminds the people they were carried out of Egypt on eagles' wings.
